Thirty Disks,
Thirty Names

A toy that says an animal's name when you set a coded disk on its peg. Thirty printed disks laid out on the carpet, picked up one at a time, and a phone recording the whole thing. Somewhere in those 97 seconds is the mapping from code to animal — which disk says what — and nothing in the video states it. This is how it was pulled out.

WHY

Nothing is where it was

the obvious approach, and why it dies immediately

The instinct is to subtract one frame from the next and see which pink circle disappeared. That fails on the first pair. The camera is handheld and pans and zooms constantly, so a disk that never moved is hundreds of pixels away from where it was a second ago, and every pixel in the frame reads as changed.

But the floor is flat, and the disks do not move. Those two facts are the whole solution: a plane viewed by a moving camera transforms by a single homography, so if the camera motion can be undone, each disk has one fixed address for the entire video.

01

Sample the video

30 fps → 5 fps · 485 frames

Disks come off the grid about once every three seconds, so five frames a second is roughly fifteen samples per event — enough to see a step without carrying six times the data. Frame N is at t = (N−1)/5 and that stays true for the rest of the pipeline.

02

Tell pink from carpet

score = (R−G) + ½(B−G)

A per-pixel score, not a classifier. Pink PLA is red-heavy and blue-heavy; the carpet is neither. The second term is there because of the hand: skin is also red-heavy, so R−G alone confuses the two, but skin is blue-poor where the disks are blue-rich.

patchR−GB−Gscore
disk56.6+21.567.3
skin35.1−7.931.1
carpet5.5−10.90.1

The blue term widens the disk-to-skin margin from 21.5 to 36.2, which helps — but be honest about what it does not do. Skin still lands at 31, essentially on the threshold. A hand resting over a disk is genuinely ambiguous to this feature, and no amount of channel arithmetic fixes it. That problem gets solved later, in time rather than in color (step 07).

03

Find the thirty centers, once

frame 0001 only · pitch 158 px · radius ~75 px

Only the opening frame needs this, because after registration every other frame borrows its answer. Two standard tools were tried first and both failed for reasons worth keeping.

Dead end — circle detection

HoughCircles never returns 30. The disk rims are low-contrast pink against pink; loosen the accumulator and it finds 215 circles, tighten it and it finds 4. There is no setting in between where the count is stable.

Dead end — connected components

Color thresholding returns one blob, not thirty. The disks are laid out touching each other, so every pink pixel is in the same component. Nothing about the mask knows where one disk ends.

What works is a matched filter that encodes exactly that shape: mean score inside a 48 px disc minus mean score in an 82–100 px annulus. At a true center the middle is pink and the ring catches the seams and the carpet between neighbors; anywhere else the two terms cancel.

Peak-picking alone still wanders, because a peak can be soft and a neighbor's rim can be sharp. So the picking is regularised by what we know about the arrangement: it is a 6×5 lattice on a plane. Snap every point to its local maximum, fit a homography from lattice index (row, col) to image position by RANSAC, re-project, repeat. The homography drags outliers back onto the grid. Three rounds took the median residual from 17 px to 9 px.

04

Undo the camera

SIFT at ½ scale · Lowe ratio 0.75 · RANSAC 6 px

For every frame: detect SIFT keypoints, match them to frame 0001, and fit a homography with RANSAC. The unglamorous hero here is the carpet pile — dense, high-contrast, non-repeating texture, which is exactly what a feature detector wants. A clean floor would have been much harder.

Frames that could not reach 18 inliers were dropped rather than trusted — 26 of 485, mostly motion blur while the phone swung. A bad homography is worse than a missing sample, because it silently points a disk's address at its neighbor.

05

Sample presence — in three states

median score in a 30 px disc at each warped center

Warp the thirty fixed centers into the frame and take the median score in a small disc at each. The outcome has three values, and the third is the one that matters: present, absent, or unknown. If a warped center lands outside the frame, that disk is off-screen, not gone. Conflating those two is the bug that would sink the whole thing — the camera leaves half the grid for seconds at a time, and every one of those disks would read as removed.

06

Calibrate on the ends

t < 0.6 s: all present · t > 94 s: all gone

The video hands you both labels for free. At the start everything is on the carpet; at the end nothing is. Score the two windows and the distribution is flatly bimodal — present runs 60 to 130, absent runs 0 to 2.5, and there is nothing in between.

07

Find each disappearance

first t where the next 8 s are ≥75% absent
Dead end — “last time it was seen”

Registration slop resurrects dead disks. A homography that is a few pixels off puts a removed disk's address on the rim of a neighbor that is still there, so a disk that left at 10 s produces stray hits at 60 s. Taking the last positive sample dated every removal far too late, and bunched five of them onto the same instant.

The fix is to stop asking when it was last seen and start asking when it was reliably gone: the earliest moment where at least 75% of the next 8 seconds of in-frame samples are absent, having been mostly present in the 3 seconds before. Isolated false positives cannot move that boundary, and — this is where step 02's honesty gets repaid — neither can a hand hovering over a disk before the grab.

08

The check nobody designed in

the order came out row-major

Sort the thirty disks by the step time and they come out in reading order: left to right, top to bottom, one row after another. Nothing in the pipeline knows the grid has rows. The lattice indices were only ever used to regularise a fit, and the disappearance times were computed independently per disk from raw pixels.

Getting reading order out the far end is the strongest evidence the chain is sound — and it earned its keep immediately, because two disks (29 and 19) had steps only 0.6 s apart. Their raw order was ambiguous; the row-major pattern settles it.

09

Pair with the audio — by order, not by time

faster-whisper large-v3, word timestamps

The soundtrack gives thirty animal names with timestamps. The tempting move is to attach each name to the nearest pick. That is wrong, and quietly so. The lag from picking a disk up to hearing its animal wanders from −1.2 s to +6.7 s, because he reaches for the next disk while the toy is still talking — and that spread is wider than the three-second cadence, so nearest-in-time assigns names to the wrong events without ever looking implausible.

Order survives all of it. Two strictly increasing sequences of the same length admit exactly one order-preserving pairing, so counting is the entire argument. Which makes the count worth defending: the five gaps where nothing was transcribed were re-listened to individually, and each held only words already accounted for. Thirty disks, thirty names, no spares.

What each code says

arranged as they sat on the carpet

Confirmed against the toy afterwards. Two entries recorded earlier from a ten-disk bench test turned out to be misheard — 14 is kangaroo, not koala, and 24 is zebra, not whale — which is its own small lesson about single trials.

Code 6 is still open. It was not in the lineup filmed, so the toy has never been asked. Print it, set it on the peg, listen.

And the one thing the pipeline could not do: the disk at row 3, column 2 reads as either 6 or 9. The generator sets numerals in a face whose 6 and 9 are point-symmetric, the disk was lying rotated, and there is no underline to break the tie. A person who owned the set answered it in four seconds. It is 9, and it says tiger.
